A federal judge in California has blocked a Department of Homeland Security effort to identify noncitizens on voter rolls. White House correspondent Liz Landers reports. Geoff Bennett: With a proper welcome to the "News Hour" now, we should say we had a technical issue at the start of tonight's broadcast. So thank you for bearing with us. Now, with the midterm elections less than two weeks away, a new legal battle is raising questions about the federal government's role in policing who is eligible to vote. A federal judge in California has blocked a Department of Homeland Security effort to identify noncitizens on voter rolls. I spoke earlier about it with our White House correspondent, Liz Landers. So, Liz, this federal judge issued this ruling with now less than two weeks before Election Day. So there's some clear urgency here. Liz Landers: Yes, the Department of Homeland Security has been engaged in this operation since August, according to this lawsuit. And this federal judge in California ruled yesterday that they must restrict their field operations to look for voter fraud and noncitizens on voter rolls. DHS cannot do stops in field interviews unless they think someone is a noncitizen. This applies to nine different states, California, Connecticut, Georgia, Missouri, Nevada, New York, Pennsylvania, Washington, and Wisconsin. There are hundreds of DHS agents who are assigned across all states to look for voter fraud. This has been dubbed the Unlawful Voter Initiative. And the judge here is concerned that the lists created by DHS had errors and did have citizens' names on them.
